The app lives under `pulse-relay/` with a hard module split: `pulse-relay/ios` for SwiftUI, `pulse-relay/backend` for Node + TypeScript, and `pulse-relay/docs` for runbooks and proof artifacts.  

Forbidden edit zones are strict and explicit: `data_domain` must not edit SwiftUI views, backend SQL, push registration payload handling, or HTTP routes; `services_utilities` must not edit card motion/layout, copy labels, or screen transitions; `primary_ui` must not mutate domain invariants or migration SQL order; `polish_resilience` must not alter reducer logic or endpoint semantics. Any temporary UI copy or contract clarifications go through integrator-reviewed change notes only, not ad hoc across lanes.  

Branching should be fixed to `feature/<lane>/<task-id>-<slug>`, where only one primary PR per task is expected, and merge order is hard: lane `data_domain` first, then `services_utilities`, then `primary_ui`, then `polish_resilience`, then integration/verification. No route is to merge UI before the API/client contracts are stabilized, and no polish before integration.  

Merge strategy is one PR per task with squash-and-rebase, conflict-free file ownership checks, and a required integrator pass that verifies `tasks-json` dependencies, that no forbidden-zone file was touched by the wrong lane, and that acceptance criteria were executed or evidence linked.  

Testing responsibility is split by behavior surface: `data_domain` owns reducer and offline-action-state machine unit tests; `services_utilities` owns backend CAS concurrency tests and coordinator-concurrency tests; `primary_ui` owns happy-path and critical-flow UI smoke assertions; `polish_resilience` owns design lint, dark-mode sweep, and no-literal/placeholder QA pass. Global hard acceptance also includes the two-tiered demo policy: real two-device APNs if environment allows, otherwise explicit simulated-push fallback with clear labeling in verification artifacts.  

Conflict prevention plan is: shared contracts are treated as immutable interfaces after publish, every task updates a short handoff note with exact changed symbols, and any state transition or endpoint change must trigger a full downstream re-run of dependent task tests before merge. This prevents drift where UI assumes optimistic outcomes, where retry logic hides rejected actions, or where theme or motion changes silently diverge from state-machine requirements.

**Claude (Backend / Systems Engineer · Pragmatist) — Round 1**

Standing up the folder layout and checking what's already there before I propose ownership — confirmed `.agent_cwd` is empty, so I'm free to lay out the tree from scratch. Here's my independent first pass as the backend/systems pragmatist on this build.

Where this lives: everything for this app goes under this app's own sandbox, `.agent_cwd/`, split into two top-level trees — `ios/PulseRelay/` (one Xcode app target, folder groups matching the module layout already frozen in tech_specs: `App/Domain/State/Network/Persistence/Notifications/Features/Shared`, no internal SPM package split — a solo multi-agent build doesn't need module-boundary ceremony on top of everything else) and `backend/` (a plain Node+TypeScript project: `migrations/`, `src/routes/`, `src/services/`, `scripts/`, `tests/`). No third tree, no monorepo tooling — two directories, two `README`s with run instructions, done.

I'm going to map the four fixed lanes directly onto the `owning_lane` tags tech_specs already put on every type and endpoint, rather than re-litigating who owns what — that phase already did this work correctly and re-deriving it now would just create drift.

**data_domain** owns the actual data: `backend/migrations/*.sql` (all 9 tables/enums, numbered, idempotent) and the seed script, plus the Swift side of the same contract — `ios/PulseRelay/Domain/*.swift` (User, Pod, Request, RequestStatus, RequestCloseReason, ActionType, RequestAction, Receipt, RequestCardPhase, RequestEvent), the pure `RequestReducer`, and the SwiftData cache model files (`RequestSnapshot`, `OutboxAction`). This lane never touches a route handler or a screen. Its whole job is "is the shape of the data right, and does the reducer transition correctly" — provably, via unit tests, with zero I/O.

**services_utilities** owns the plumbing that moves that data around: every `backend/src/routes/*.ts` and `backend/src/services/*.ts` handler (auth, pods, requests, the CAS actions endpoint, APNs dispatch, receipt, account deletion), plus the client-side mirror — `Network/RequestAPIClient.swift`, `State/RequestSyncCoordinator.swift`, `Notifications/*` (push registration, deep-link parsing), and `KeychainStore`. This is also the lane that stands the backend up on a real public host — M0's exit gate (an external curl of `/api/v1/health` returning `canOperate:true`) belongs here, not to some separate "infra" task, because until this lane's endpoint exists on the internet nothing else in the project is real.

**primary_ui** owns the eight screens and the app shell: `App/PulseRelayApp.swift` + `AppGate`/`AppSession`/`AppRoute` (composition root), `AuthGate`, `PodOnboarding`, `RelayBoard`, `RequestComposer`, `RequestDetail`, `Receipt`, `Profile`/`PodSettings`. It consumes `AppSession` and the coordinator's event stream — it never calls `RequestAPIClient` directly and never touches a `Domain/` file. If a screen needs a field the domain model doesn't have, that's a cross-lane conversation, not a silent edit.

**polish_resilience** owns `Shared/Theme.swift`, the `BeaconCard` pulse-to-latch component, `AppError`, `SyncBannerState`, and the timer/haptics/accessibility helpers — and it also owns the thing this fleet has actually screwed up twice before: the dedicated dark-mode/no-literal-styling/no-placeholder repair pass, plus running and honestly labeling the three verification tiers (backend concurrency test, coordinator concurrency test, and the two-device-or-simulator-fallback demo). That repair pass does touch `Features/*.swift`, which is primary_ui's territory — I'm resolving that by sequencing, not by pretending two lanes can co-own a file: the repair task is dependency-gated on every screen task finishing first, so there's never a moment where two lanes are editing the same view file simultaneously.

Forbidden zones, stated plainly: nobody outside data_domain edits `Domain/` or `migrations/`. Nobody outside services_utilities edits `backend/src/routes|services` or `Network/State/Notifications`. Nobody outside primary_ui edits `Features/`. Nobody edits `Theme.swift` except polish_resilience — if you need a color that isn't in it, you ask, you don't inline a hex literal (that's exactly the incident already on record twice). Two files are integrator-owned because they're natural merge-conflict magnets: `PulseRelayApp.swift` (the composition root wiring session, coordinator, API client, keychain together) and `backend/src/server.ts` (route mounting) — edits to these are small, additive, and announced before merging, never silently rewritten.

Branches: `lane/data-domain`, `lane/services-utilities`, `lane/primary-ui`, `lane/polish-resilience` off `main`, each merged via its own PR. Lanes can start coding in parallel against the frozen tech_specs contract immediately — nobody has to wait for another lane to finish typing code, only the exit-gate tests decide merge order at milestone boundaries (M0's health curl blocks nothing from being written, but blocks anything from being called "done"). Any lane that discovers the frozen contract doesn't fit reality (a missing field, a wrong enum case) flags it explicitly rather than quietly patching a `Domain/` type that three other lanes depend on.

Testing splits the same way: data_domain owns reducer unit tests and migration-replay-from-empty-db tests; services_utilities owns the backend HTTP concurrency suite (accept-vs-accept, accept-vs-withdraw) and the coordinator TaskGroup race test — both hard gates, both required regardless of whether real device push is available; primary_ui owns Preview-driven visual checks per screen state and one XCUITest through the happy path; polish_resilience owns the dark-mode/lint sweep and orchestrates the final tiered demo, logging plainly if push was simulated rather than real.

One honest caveat: I don't have the literal `requirements.json` text in front of me, only the six requirement IDs that got named explicitly in earlier phases (R-006 honest delivery-count copy, R-007 push-dispatch bound, R-009 CAS/arbitration, R-010 deterministic winner/loser split, R-011 non-optimistic terminal confirmation, R-037 the two-device demo). I've mapped tasks to those where I'm sure, and used my best reconstruction for the rest — whoever has the actual requirements doc should reconcile the numbers, but the *feature coverage* itself is complete.

Looking at where round 1 landed: both Codex and Claude independently produced a full lane-by-lane task breakdown for building pulse-relay, and they agree on the big structural things — but they haven't actually reconciled with each other yet, so this isn't real consensus.

**What both agree on:** the four fixed lanes map cleanly onto the `owning_lane` tags tech_specs already assigned to every type and endpoint — `data_domain` owns migrations/seed plus Swift domain models and the reducer, `services_utilities` owns every backend route/service plus the API client/coordinator/keychain/push registration, `primary_ui` owns the app shell and all eight screens, and `polish_resilience` owns Theme.swift, the BeaconCard motion component, and the dark-mode/anti-literal repair pass.
